title: Cataract Surgery in the High Myope
summary: Mastering the 'Big Eye': A comprehensive guide to managing eyes with axial lengths >26.0mm. From advanced biometry formulas to preventing reverse pupillary block and mitigating the lifelong risk of retinal detachment.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Epidemiology
content: High Myopia: Defined as spherical equivalent ≤ -6.00 D or Axial Length (AL) ≥ 26.0 mm.
Pathologic Myopia: High myopia with associated degenerative changes (staphyloma, lacquer cracks, etc.).
Prevalence: Affects 1-3% of the global population; rising significantly in East Asia.
Cataract Onset: High myopes typically develop nuclear sclerotic and posterior subcapsular cataracts 10-15 years earlier than emmetropes.

rows: Commonly used; tends to result in hyperopic surprise in very long eyes without adjustment.
Regression adjustment applied to AL to improve accuracy of SRK/T and Holladay 1.
Highly accurate; accounts for the 'effective lens position' more effectively.
Current gold standard; uses big data/AI to minimize outliers in extreme AL.
Uses posterior corneal curvature; vital if the patient had prior LASIK/PRK.

sections.title: The Pathophysiology of Reverse Pupillary Block
content: 1. Infusion of BSS creates high pressure in the Anterior Chamber (AC).
2. Fluid pushes iris 360 degrees against the lens capsule.
3. A 'one-way valve' is created; fluid cannot flow back to the AC.
4. Sudden extreme deepening of the AC occurs with intense pain.
5. Management: Gently lift iris edge with a second instrument to equalize pressure.

sections.title: Surgical Technique Pearls
content: Incision: Construct longer tunnels to prevent 'floppy iris syndrome' and iris prolapse.
Capsulorhexis: Aim for 5.0 - 5.5mm. Too small increases risk of capsular phimosis; too large allows IOL tilt.
Hydrodissection: Be gentle; high myopes have thin posterior capsules and liquefied vitreous (reduced support).
Phaco Power: Lower parameters needed as the nucleus is often softer than expected, but beware of 'Brunescent' surprises.
Stability: Use a Capsular Tension Ring (CTR) if there is any sign of zonular laxity or to stabilize a large bag.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Hazards
content: Sudden Loss of Red Reflex: Possible suprachoroidal hemorrhage (increased risk in high myopes).
Iris-Lens Diaphragm Retraction: Sign of Reverse Pupillary Block.
Globe Perforation: During peribulbar or retrobulbar block (Staphyloma makes AL unpredictable).
Post-op 'Flashers and Floaters': Mandatory dilated fundus exam to rule out retinal tears.

rows: May require specialized ordering (e.g., -5.0 to +5.0 D).
Lower rates of PCO and less inflammatory.
Better stability in large capsular bags compared to plate-haptic IOLs.
High risk of dissatisfaction due to macular pathology or higher RD risk later.
High myopes often prefer some 'near' vision and find sudden emmetropia jarring.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Post-Op Vision Loss

content.explanation: M: Macular check (OCT essential). Y: Yield (low) IOL powers. O: Open the iris (Reverse block). P: Periphery (Retinal exam). I: Instruments (Longer reach). A: Accuracy (Barrett/Kane formulas).

sections.title: Landmark Insights: Evidence-Based Data
content: The 'AL Adjustment' (Wang-Koch): Highlighted that AL overestimation is a primary cause of hyperopic surprise (2011).
RD Risk Timeline: Risk remains elevated for up to 20 years post-operatively, peaking in the first 2-3 years.
YAG Capsulotomy: Increases the risk of RD in high myopes; perform only when clinically essential.
Refractive Neutrality: Studies show high myopes with AL >29mm have the highest variance in IOL formula performance.

sections.title: Post-operative Management Protocol
content: 1. Day 1: IOP check (High myopes prone to steroid response).
2. Week 1: Dilated fundus exam to inspect peripheral retina.
3. Month 1: Final refraction and OCT Macula to rule out CME/CNV.
4. Ongoing: Annual dilated exams for the life of the patient.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Always check for a 'Posterior Staphyloma' on B-scan if biometry is inconsistent.
Consider Topical Anesthesia to avoid the risk of globe perforation with needles.
Keep a cohesive OVD (like Healon) ready to maintain the chamber during IOL insertion.
Warn patients pre-operatively that they may see 'floaters' more clearly once the cataract is removed.
